session_title: Old injury recurrence and problem description
theme: 健康-野外工作者的膝伤康复

content.text: Ye Lu, after the recent load-bearing survey, my old left knee injury flared up again, and it hurts a lot when going up and down slopes. This was taken at the camp today, and it's a bit red and swollen.
Shiyan, this looks quite serious. Have you been diagnosed by a doctor before? For example, issues with the meniscus or ligaments?

Well, years ago, after a climbing injury, I was diagnosed with cartilage wear. The doctor advised avoiding excessive weight-bearing and impact, but given the nature of this job, you know, it's hard to avoid completely.

I understand, just like the time I carried photography equipment over a long distance and ended up with shoulder and neck strain. I improved a lot later through specific stretching and strengthening exercises. Do you usually do exercises targeting the muscles around your knee joint, such as the quadriceps and hamstrings?
I haven't done enough in this regard, mainly relying on sheer willpower. When work gets busy, I just can't manage to focus on these things.
This won't do. Safety first, just like you always remind me. If we don't address the knee issue properly, it will affect your fieldwork even more in the future.
You're right. During recent surveys, I've had to slow down a lot on both uphill and downhill sections, which has reduced efficiency and worried the team.
Check this out. I've compiled some lightweight gear ideas that might help reduce your load, just like how we optimized our hiking equipment before.
Thank you, the design of this backpack is indeed more reasonable. However, for knee issues, simply reducing weight might not be enough; I need to find some practical relief methods.
Yes, there are many non-medication or non-surgical methods. For example, I can share some stretching movements and strengthening exercises that I learned during my shoulder and neck rehabilitation.
Okay, I'm willing to learn. Practicality comes first—as long as it allows me to keep working.
First, you can perform wall sits daily to strengthen the quadriceps, as well as leg curls to exercise the hamstrings. These exercises help stabilize the knee joint.
Wall squat? Sounds simple, let me give it a try. But what should I do if my knees hurt after a long hike in the wild?
During the acute phase, you can apply cold compresses and rest as shown in your picture. In daily life, use trekking poles to share the load, just as we emphasize during valley hikes.
Hmm, I've been using trekking poles all along, but maybe my posture isn't right. Could you help me check it next time?

Of course. Look, this is the mountain scenery I captured last time. My knees were fine then, but the strain in my shoulders and neck made me realize the importance of recovery. Nature is beautiful, but we also need to take good care of ourselves.
This photo is really nice, capturing the moment perfectly. You're right, respecting nature also includes protecting ourselves. I'll start doing these exercises.

Great! We can regularly communicate about our progress, just like the team collaboration we planned for hiking. Now that your knee is better, you can take me to more places for shooting in the future.
Haha, okay. Stability is more important than speed, and this time I need to apply that to myself. Thanks for the advice, Yelu.
You're welcome, Shi Yan. Stay in touch, and let me know if you have any questions. Safety first—let's work together!
